title: Performance Budgets
summary: Defining hard limits on bundle size and user-facing metrics like LCP and TTI, enforcing them in CI, and code-splitting as the primary lever for staying under budget.

slides.markdown:
"Keep it fast" is not enforceable — a **performance budget** is. A budget is a hard, measurable limit (a bundle size in KB, a Largest Contentful Paint in milliseconds) tied to a real user-facing metric, checked automatically so a PR that blows it fails the same way a broken test fails.

This topic covers what to budget, how to enforce it in CI rather than by vigilance, and the main lever for staying under budget — code-splitting — plus the trap every team eventually hits: setting a budget once and never revisiting it as the app legitimately grows.

slides.sectionTitle: What a performance budget actually is
slides.markdown:
A performance budget is a **numeric limit tied to a user-facing consequence**, not an aspiration. "Try to keep the bundle small" is a value; "the main JS bundle must stay under 170KB gzipped, because past that our mid-tier Android test device misses the 2.5s LCP target" is a budget — it has a number, a unit, and a reason.

The reason matters more than the number: a budget derived from an actual measured device/network condition (not an arbitrary round number) is defensible when someone asks to bust it for a new feature, and gives you a real answer to "why 170 and not 200." A budget with no story behind its number gets negotiated away the first time it's inconvenient.

slides.subTitle: Bundle size, TTI, LCP, request count
slides.markdown:
Four metrics cover most of what teams budget in practice:

- **Bundle size** — the compressed (gzip/brotli) size of JS shipped for a route. Easiest to measure and enforce, but a proxy — a small bundle full of blocking synchronous work can still render slowly.
- **LCP (Largest Contentful Paint)** — when the largest visible element (often a hero image or headline) finishes rendering. Google's Core Web Vitals threshold: under 2.5s is "good."
- **TTI (Time to Interactive)** — when the page can reliably respond to input without a long main-thread task blocking it. A page can look done (good LCP) and still be unresponsive to a tap for another second.
- **Request count** — how many separate network round trips a page's initial load makes; each one costs latency even if small, especially over a slow or high-latency mobile connection.

Bundle size is the easiest lever to control directly (this topic's focus), but LCP and TTI are the metrics users actually feel — a team that only budgets bundle size can hit its number while shipping a slow page.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: tracking bundle size per PR
slides.markdown:
A budget only holds if the trend is visible before it's blown, not discovered after. A per-PR bundle-size report — bot-posted as a comment showing the diff versus the base branch — turns an invisible, gradual creep into a number every reviewer sees on every change, the same way a diff shows added and removed lines.

The trend view matters as much as the single-PR diff: a bundle that grows 2KB per PR looks harmless in any one review, but 2KB × 200 merged PRs a quarter is 400KB — well past most mobile budgets — and only a tracked-over-time chart makes that visible before it's a crisis.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: enforcing a budget in CI

slides.markdown:
| | Route-based | Component-based |
|---|---|---|
| Split unit | An entire page/route | A single heavy component (a rich-text editor, a chart library) |
| Best for | Reducing initial load for pages users don't always visit | A specific known-heavy dependency used on only some interactions within a page |
| Granularity | Coarse — easy to reason about, big wins | Fine — more surgical, more chunks to manage |
| Common trigger | "Users on the home page shouldn't download checkout's code" | "This one modal pulls in a 200KB charting library only 5% of users open" |

**How to decide:** always do route-based splitting first — it's the highest-leverage, lowest-effort win. Add component-based splitting only for specific dependencies you can name and measure (a chart library, a rich editor), not as a blanket policy, since over-splitting adds request overhead of its own.

slides.sectionTitle: When splitting isn't enough: what else eats budget
slides.markdown:
Code-splitting reduces what's downloaded *per route*, but three other costs commonly blow a budget even with good splitting: **duplicated dependencies** across chunks (two lazy-loaded routes each bundling their own copy of a date library because the bundler didn't dedupe them), **polyfills shipped to everyone** (a `core-js` polyfill for a browser feature 95% of users' browsers already support natively, sent to 100% of users anyway), and **third-party scripts** (analytics, a chat widget, an ad SDK) that the team doesn't control and that often dwarf the app's own code.

A senior-level performance budget conversation names these three explicitly rather than assuming code-splitting alone solves the number — bundler analysis tools (`webpack-bundle-analyzer`, `source-map-explorer`) exist specifically to surface duplication and oversized third-party scripts that splitting doesn't touch.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: setting a budget once and never revisiting it
slides.markdown:
**Wrong pattern:** a team sets a 170KB budget at launch, wires it into CI, and considers performance solved. Two years later every PR either fails the check and gets a one-off exception approved, or the budget got bumped to 250KB "just this once" three separate times with no reassessment of whether devices or user expectations changed.

**Why it happens:** a budget is easy to set and easy to forget, especially once it's automated — automation removes the human check-in that would otherwise prompt "is 170KB still the right number."

**Correct model:** revisit the budget on a schedule (quarterly is common) against real data — has the target device mix shifted, has the network-condition assumption changed, has a legitimate new feature genuinely earned more budget. A budget that only ever gets exceptions granted, never renegotiated with evidence, has stopped functioning as a budget at all.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagnosing budget regression before fixing it
slides.markdown:
When a bundle has drifted well past its budget over time, the senior move isn't a single fix — it's diagnosis first. Pull the bundle-analyzer output and separate the growth into buckets: legitimate new features, duplicated dependencies, and unmaintained third-party scripts. Each bucket has a different fix.

For legitimate feature growth, the honest move is often accepting a higher budget for the routes that earned it while keeping the shared `main` chunk's budget strict — a new feature's code shouldn't inflate a bundle that loads on every route. For duplication, dedupe via the bundler or a shared-dependency policy (echoing the shared-singleton problem from micro-frontends). For third-party scripts, negotiate with whoever owns that vendor relationship — engineering often can't unilaterally remove an analytics SDK product or legal requires.

The closing move: re-baseline the budget from the diagnosis, not from the current bloated number — a budget reset to "whatever we're at now" isn't a budget, it's a rubber stamp.
